sentences: You are standing in front of the Hall of Public Audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648 and held his first darbar here soon after.
The hall is eighty feet long and forty feet deep, all of it red sandstone, and it once carried gilding and painted stucco that has long since gone.
Three aisles of seven bays each, and every bay is four columns holding an engrailed arch.
In the middle of the far wall there is a recess about twenty one feet across, raised above the floor, and that is where the Emperor sat.
The lawn in front of you stands in for a courtyard five hundred and sixty feet long.
The shrubberies at its edges mark where the arcades ran, and every morning those arcades were full of men waiting to be seen.
This is the Rang Mahal, the painted palace.
It is named for the colour that once covered the inside of these walls, and almost none of it is left.
In the time of Shah Jahan it was called the Imtiyaz Mahal, the palace of distinction, and it was the largest apartment of the imperial household.
A marble channel runs the length of the floor, and at its centre sits a basin cut from a single block of Makrana marble, ten feet by nine.
The ceiling was silver first, then copper, then wood, each replacement a smaller claim than the one before.
Behind you, between this hall and the back of the Diwan-i-Aam, there was a walled garden with a tank at its centre.
It lay buried until 1911, when it was uncovered again.
The Hall of Private Audience.
Ninety feet by sixty seven, on a plinth four and a half feet high, and by one nineteenth century judgement the most heavily ornamented thing Shah Jahan ever built.
The lower parts of these piers are inlaid with coloured stone, each piece cut to fit a socket chiselled out of the marble.
The upper parts were gilded and painted.
Down the centre of the floor runs a marble channel twelve feet wide, called the Nahr-i-Bihisht, the stream of paradise.
On the dais in this room stood the peacock throne, until Nadir Shah carried it away to Persia in 1739.
He took the submission of the Mughal Emperor in this room first, and the throne afterwards.
